extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers studying narratology and narrative technique (esp. Proust and prose fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for classifying and using retrospective (analepsis/recall) and anticipatory (prolepsis) narrative moves: types, functions, scope (reach vs. extent), junction strategies, and effects (deferred significance, migration, overlap). Illustrated chiefly with Proust and classic epic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analepsis: external vs internal (classification by reach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analepses are divided into classes depending on whether the point to which they reach is located outside or inside the temporal field of the first narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External analepses reach to moments outside the first narrative's temporal frame; internal analepses reach to points inside that frame. This distinction underpins further categories (partial/complete/mixed) and affects how the analepsis connects back to the primary narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative analepsis (class-level retrospection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analepsis that refers to a class (e.g., 'a winter') rather than a specific individual occurrence (a given winter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the retrospective fills an ellipsis for a repeated series of events (e.g., describing 'all the previous dinners' through a single dinner). Especially effective when the analepsis itself must be iterative; creates synthetic coverage of a whole series with condensed tense (imperfect for repeated action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating analepses / 'recalls' (internal homodiegetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal homodiegetic analepses that openly retrace the narrative's own path; called repeating analepses or 'recalls.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically limited in textual dimension (allusions or retroceptions) but important for narrative economy (notably in Proust). They often present as brief allusions to earlier narrative moments and can function to re-present, re-evaluate, or link past episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recalls via involuntary memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalls produced by involuntary memory (e.g., the madeleine) that refer to an earlier time in the narrative and prompt a retrospective section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recalls are often 'deliberately chosen or devised because of their casual and commonplace character' and suggest comparisons between present and past; their affect is typically euphoric even if the revived past was painful. Examples: Proust's three reminiscences during the Guermantes matinee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recalls motivated by analogy (comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalls triggered when a present situation reminds the narrator of an earlier, similar situation—accent on analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function is to invite comparison and to place two similar-but-different situations in dialogue (example: Duc de Guermantes's words reminding the hero of identical words earlier). Effective for thematic echoes and linkage across episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recalls motivated by contrast (recognition/contrast function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalls where present perception highlights contrast with an earlier episode, often producing recognition (e.g., identifying a prostitute seen earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recalls can be obsessive in precision, establishing direct communication between sections and sometimes producing narrative 'migration' or 'scattering' (interpolation that seems snatched from earlier text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recalls that retrofit or modify past meaning (deferred/postponed significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalls whose principal function is to modify the meaning of past occurrences after the event—either making significant what was not originally so or refuting an initial interpretation and replacing it with a new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'deferred or postponed significance'; ties into mechanisms of enigma (Barthes' S/Z). Examples: the syringas incident whose 'cruel significance' 'entirely escaped' the narrator until later; later revelations (Andree/Albertine) supply the clue and change the interpretation. This is a core Proustian technique for circulating meaning and achieving reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Migration / narrative scattering
rubrics_metrics.description: When material from an earlier section is interpolated almost verbatim into a later section (so that the later section seems to have snatched text from the earlier narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as migration or narrative scattering; creates a feeling of direct communication between sections (example: variant lines about 'Rachel' appearing almost verbatim in Guermantes). It can produce a sense of obsessive precision and tie sections tightly together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial analepsis (pinpointed retrospection ending in ellipsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An analeptic episode whose extent is much less than its reach and which ends on an ellipsis without rejoining the first narrative (it supplies an isolated piece of past information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves to provide a discrete piece of information needed for understanding a specific present moment (example: Ulysses' wound). The analepsis interrupts, then the first narrative resumes, often without an explicit linking, sometimes resumed implicitly or with an explanatory formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete analepsis (rejoins the first narrative at its start)
rubrics_metrics.description: An analepsis that goes back as far as the relevant beginning (e.g., fall of Troy) and then carries along to rejoin the first narrative—covering antecedents comprehensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to in medias res practice; can form a major part of the narrative (examples: Ulysses' narration before the Phaeacians; novels where the analepsis constitutes the chief portion and the first narrative functions as denouement in advance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed analepsis (external prolonged to rejoin/past the starting point)
rubrics_metrics.description: External analepses prolonged so they rejoin and even pass beyond the starting point of the first narrative; determined by extent rather than reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not much resorted to but possible; extent controls this mixed class. Example: Des Grieux's narrative is 'mixed' in that it rejoins the first narrative not at the beginning but where the first was interrupted (a round trip of extent equal to reach in some versions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete internal analepsis (extent equals reach; round trip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal analepses whose extent is rigorously equal to their reach and which bring the retrospective narrative up to the moment the first narrative was interrupted—completing a 'perfect round trip.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Les Souffrances de l'inventeur where the retrospective is brought to the moment when David's and Lucien's destinies meet. This creates a tight circular narrative movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent vs. reach as controlling distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent (how much narrative is covered) and reach (how far back in time the analepsis goes) jointly control the taxonomy of retrospections (partial/complete/mixed/internal/external).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical principle: differences in extent relative to reach determine whether an analepsis is partial, complete, mixed, internal, or external, and influence junction behavior and narrative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resumption strategies: explicit resumptions ('this is why')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some narratives openly acknowledge the end of analepsis with explicit resumptions (formulae like 'this is why' or 'the feelings ... should now be understood').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzacian explicit resumptions clarify the explanatory function and make the return to the main narrative overt; Proust sometimes imitates or parodies this; useful where the author wants to signal interpretive closure of the retrospective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resumption strategies: elliptical / discreet resumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resumptions that are highly discreet or elliptical—returning to the present with little or no explicit transitional marker (e.g., a paragraph break or a subtle phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in Proust: sometimes only a paragraph break separates analepsis from resumed narrative, or a simple offhand phrase effects the transition, increasing the elliptical feel and underlining temporal rupture by asyndeton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling overlap / juncture awkwardness (overlap management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete analepses necessarily create overlap at the junction; if mishandled this produces incoherence, but skillful handling can convert awkwardness into charm or decorative effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cesar Birotteau shows awkward overlap; Les Souffrances de l'inventeur extracts a decorative/time-play element to turn the overlap into humor. Authors may explicitly coordinate the return, craft decorative linking, or use playful masking to smooth overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliding the juncture (dissimulation or forgetting of analepsis end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques by which the narrative avoids acknowledging its own juncture—dissimulating the end of analepsis, pretending not to know it has been reached, or even forgetting the analeptic character and prolonging it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proustian typical behavior: the narrative may avoid naming the resumption, may continue the analepsis without signaling the return, or may dissimulate by appearing offhand. Example: Combray where Swann is named earlier but later the link is made as if the narrator hadn't signaled the visit before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepsis (temporal anticipation) and its rarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation or temporal prolepsis is less frequent than analepsis in Western narrative tradition, though some epics/narratives open with anticipatory summaries (plot of predestination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical novel conventions and the 'narrator-discovering-as-he-tells' ideal make prolepses rarer in Balzac, Dickens, Tolstoy. Yet some works (Manon Lescaut, The Death of Ivan Ilych) use predestination or epilogue openings that function as proleptic signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepses: internal vs external and function as epilogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses can be internal or external relative to the temporal field of the first narrative; external prolepses often function as epilogues continuing lines of action to their logical later conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Recherche, many anticipatory episodes are external prolepses that serve to narrate later events (Charlus's death, marriages, appearances years after a matinee). These often serve closure or evaluate future significance from the vantage point of narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narrative predisposition to prolepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person retrospective narration lends itself to anticipation because the narrator already inhabits a present situation and may allude to his future state as part of his role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rousseau's polemicizing retrospective voice and Robinson Crusoe's claims about his father's 'prophetic' lecture. Proust's Recherche uses prolepsis extensively precisely because of the retrospective first-person stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analepses/prolepses with extent greater than reach (transformation into anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where the analepsis continues so far beyond its original reach that it covertly transforms into a prolepsis or anticipation (extent much greater than reach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Noms de pays: le pays, where an analepsis continues to the last line of the Recherche and at an undetermined point becomes anticipatory. Proust thus unsettles conventional narration norms, anticipating modern novel procedures.
